articles.title: A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in just 7 weeks
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that severely bleached corals can make a remarkable comeback simply by touching healthy, genetically identical corals. In laboratory experiments, dying corals regained their color and fully recovered within seven weeks, with as little as five days of contact sometimes enough to start the healing process.
articles.content:
For the first time, researchers have demonstrated that severely bleached corals can fully recover after spending just a few days in contact with healthy, genetically identical corals.

In laboratory experiments, corals that had turned white and were close to dying regained their health within seven weeks. According to a study published on October 14 in Science Advances, this represents the fastest documented recovery from coral bleaching. The discovery could lead to new techniques for restoring coral reefs, which some estimates suggest could disappear within decades as climate change fuels increasingly severe and frequent marine heat waves.

Coral bleaching occurs when rising ocean temperatures cause corals to lose the beneficial algae living inside their tissues. These algae supply much of the energy corals depend on for growth and survival. Without them, corals lose their vibrant colors, struggle to obtain enough nourishment, and become more susceptible to harmful algae. Even when they survive, regaining their health can take months or years.

"While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet," said lead author Danny Collins, an oceans PhD student at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. "The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?"

An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a Way to Rescue Dying Corals

Although they may resemble plants or rocks, corals are animals. In most coral species, individual animals reproduce by creating genetically identical copies of themselves. These clones grow together into large colonies that form the foundation of coral reefs.

The idea for the study emerged from an unexpected observation in 2025. Steve Palumbi, a study coauthor and the Jane and Marshall Steel, Jr. Professor in Marine Sciences, noticed something unusual in his laboratory. Two fragments taken from the same coral colony, one healthy and the other bleached, had fallen against each other in an aquarium.

Where the fragments touched, the bleached coral began regaining its color. The change suggested that beneficial algae were returning to its tissues.

At roughly the same time, Collins was investigating how coral diseases develop and spread. He was particularly interested in bacteria carried by plastic debris that lands on corals and can introduce harmful microorganisms through direct contact.

"Harmful bacteria enter corals through physical contact," said Collins, who is also a Knight-Hennessy Scholar. "We were curious about what would happen if we used contact to reintroduce something good - the beneficial algae from healthy corals."

To investigate, Collins designed an experiment using 10 pairs of coral fragments. Each pair consisted of one healthy fragment and one bleached fragment originating from the same coral animal.

Five pairs were positioned so that the fragments physically touched. The other five pairs were separated by gaps measuring only a few millimeters.

The results revealed a dramatic difference. Every bleached fragment that touched its healthy counterpart recovered completely within seven weeks. In contrast, the bleached fragments that were kept apart died.

How a Simple Touch Triggers Rapid Coral Recovery

The researchers discovered that the remarkable recovery depends on a special ability of genetically identical corals to connect their tissues.

"Genetically identical corals recognize one another when they come into contact," said Palumbi, who is a professor of oceans in the Doerr School of Sustainability and of biology in the School of Humanities and Sciences. "Their tissues fuse if they are from the same clone. We see something similar in humans. Organ transplants are often successful if the donor is your identical twin."

Using a powerful microscope, Collins and his colleagues examined what happened when the coral fragments touched. They found that tiny channels within their tissues quickly lined up, forming connections that allowed materials to move between the two fragments.

Through these connections, beneficial algae and the nutrients they produce could pass from the healthy coral into the bleached one. Within just three days, researchers observed algae transferring into the damaged fragments.

The team then investigated how long the corals actually needed to remain connected. By separating pairs after different periods of contact, they discovered that a single week was enough to transfer the algae required for complete recovery. In some cases, just five days of contact produced the same result.

Remarkably, the separated corals still returned to full health within seven weeks, the same amount of time required by corals that remained connected throughout the experiment.

This finding revealed that the rapid recovery was not primarily driven by a continuing supply of algae from the healthy coral. Instead, once enough algae entered the bleached fragment, they reproduced rapidly inside their new host and restored its energy supply.

"Once beneficial algae enter bleached corals, they don't just spread out," said Palumbi. "They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals."

During the second week of contact, the beneficial algae living inside the bleached fragments doubled in number approximately every four days. That growth rate was about ten times faster than what researchers have observed in wild corals.

A Promising Breakthrough for Coral Reef Restoration

Scientists have spent decades searching for ways to protect coral reefs from rising ocean temperatures, disease, increasingly acidic seawater, and other environmental pressures.

Their efforts have included selectively breeding corals that can withstand higher temperatures, raising young corals in nurseries to rebuild damaged reefs, and transferring communities of microorganisms between corals to improve their resilience.

The new findings suggest another possibility: helping bleached corals recover quickly enough to survive the dangerous period following a marine heat wave.

"Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all," said Fiorenza Micheli, the David and Lucile Packard Professor in Marine Science and a faculty advisor of Collins. "We hope this new research will inspire solutions that keep corals healthy long enough to enable full recovery after heat waves through slower processes such as growth, reproduction, and recruitment of new colonies."

However, the researchers emphasize that their experimental approach cannot yet be used to restore reefs on a large scale. For the technique to work as demonstrated, every bleached coral would need access to a healthy, genetically identical counterpart. Finding and supplying those matches across entire reefs would be impractical.

Important questions also remain about how the recovery mechanism could be adapted for broader use.

Over the coming months, the team intends to investigate other ways to introduce beneficial algae into bleached corals without requiring them to remain physically connected to healthy fragments.

One possibility involves collecting beneficial algae from healthy corals well before marine heat waves occur. Researchers could then deliver large quantities of these algae to damaged corals after bleaching events, potentially allowing them to recover much faster.

"These new insights into how corals can naturally recover give us hope for the future," said Micheli, who also co-directs the Stanford Center for Ocean Solutions. "They open the door to what's possible and may lead to the breakthrough we need to accelerate reef restoration."

Study Authors and Research Support

Micheli also serves as a professor of oceans and (by courtesy) of biology. Both Micheli and Palumbi are senior fellows at the Woods Institute for the Environment, which is part of the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability.

Additional Stanford researchers who contributed to the study include Jana Sipkova, Nathaniel Mollica, Tom Rolander, Courtney Klepac, Gabriel Calistro, and Vanessa Barone.

Mollica is a research scientist in Stanford's Oceans Department, where Calistro works as a research assistant. Rolander is a research engineer in the Fabrication Lab at the Harold A. Miller Library at Hopkins Marine Station, which belongs to the Doerr School of Sustainability.

Sipkova is a postdoctoral scholar, while Klepac is a research scientist. Barone is an assistant professor in the Biology Department of Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences and is affiliated with Bio-X and the Maternal & Child Health Research Institute.

The Molecular and Cellular Biodiversity Imaging Center, operated by Stanford's Biology Department at Hopkins Marine Station, conducted the coral image analyses.

Financial support came from the National Science Foundation and Stanford University, including seed funding through the Big Ideas for Oceans grant program. The program is organized by the Oceans Department and the Woods Institute for the Environment within the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability.

This discovery has broad implications for coral reef restoration, which is critical for marine ecosystems worldwide threatened by climate change. The study is detailed, focused, and offers hope for accelerating coral recovery, addressing a major environmental challenge.

articles.title: Volunteers help save one of London's rarest plants
articles.summary: Tower mustard has suffered steep decline in London but has been successfully grown and replanted.
articles.content:
More than 1,000 tower mustard plants have been successfully grown and planted out by volunteers in London.

It marks a successful first year for a major community-led effort to restore one of the capital's rarest native wildflowers, vital for bees, butterflies and rare moths.

Led by Citizen Zoo and Habitats & Heritage, the tower mustard project brings together a network of land managers, community groups, conservation partners and volunteers.

The plants, grown by volunteers, are being reestablished at sites across London, in regions where tower mustard was previously known to occur.

At the core of the project are the Mighty Mustard volunteers.

In March, they attended a workshop, learned how to sow the tiny seeds, and were given their own growing equipment, including pots, seed trays and soil.

Seeds were sourced from London's last remaining tower mustard populations in Lesnes Abbey Woods in Bexley and Stain Hill Reservoir in Richmond-upon-Thames.

Charlotte Harris, nature conservation manager at Habitats & Heritage, said: "[We] are passionate about engaging people in conservation initiatives. Through this tower mustard project, we have enjoyed giving local residents the unique opportunity to get hands-on in conserving one of London's rarest plants.

"We've found the volunteers have become really attached to [them]."

Seeds have now been planted at Wimbledon Common, Hounslow Heath, Lesnes Abbey Woods and Barnes Common.

Harris added: "We are hoping that this model can be used as a blueprint for helping other rare plants with volunteer input in the same way."

The final planting day is at Hampton Court Palace's Home Park on Tuesday, where plants raised separately by the Historic Royal Palaces Gardens Team and volunteers will be used.

Botanist Dr Mark Spencer has also provided expert support throughout the project.

articles.title: How one small device is solving the apartment solar access problem
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM An Australian device that splits rooftop solar power across an entire apartment building just won the country’s top design honor. Melbourne-based Allume Energy took the 2026 Australian Good Design Award of the Year for its SolShare system, which its creators describe as a “traffic controller for solar.” The device […]
The post How one small device is solving the apartment solar access problem first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

An Australian device that splits rooftop solar power across an entire apartment building just won the country’s top design honor. Melbourne-based Allume Energy took the 2026 Australian Good Design Award of the Year for its SolShare system, which its creators describe as a “traffic controller for solar.” The device also won the sustainability award at the same ceremony, held Friday at ICC Sydney, where more than 1,000 entries competed across 13 disciplines.

Why apartment solar access matters

Homeowners with their own rooftops have driven most of the residential solar boom, but apartment dwellers have largely been on the sidelines. Individual rooftop installations don’t work well in shared buildings: the costs multiply, the wiring gets messy, and you need a separate inverter for each unit. SolShare cuts through that. One rooftop system, one installation, and the device handles distribution to each apartment automatically.

Dr. Brandon Gien, chair of Good Design Australia, called it “an amazing piece of technology” and a beautifully designed solution to a complex problem. “Millions of people live in apartments, and many have had limited access to the benefits of rooftop solar,” he said. “SolShare is a clever Australian design innovation that addresses that problem in a practical way, and it is already delivering benefits at significant scale.”

One of the world’s oldest design competitions

The Australian Good Design Awards go back to 1958. Past recipients of the top prize include the Cochlear hearing implant (2000), Marc Newson’s economy class seats for the Qantas A380 (2009), the Flow Hive beehive design (2016), and filmmaker James Cameron’s Deepsea Challenger submersible (2012). SolShare now sits in that lineup.

Other sustainability winners at the 2026 awards

The night’s other awards pointed the same way. Finnish company FabPatch won the fashion and textiles discipline for a rub-on fabric repair system. No Wrap, an Australian-designed reusable pallet securing system, and Holy Carp, a plastic-free compostable alternative to the soy-sauce fish packets in sushi packaging, both won gold in their categories.

A ceremonial gathering space at Melbourne’s City Square, designed in collaboration with Wurundjeri elders to make Woi-wurrung language visible and welcome visitors to Country, won for the built environment. Sydney Children’s Hospital’s wayfinding project replaced standard clinical signage with native animals and plants grouped into three local environments: wetlands, sand dunes, and sea cliffs.

Gien said the awards are meant to recognize design that can “bring joy to our lives, but not at the expense of the environment.” A small white box on an apartment wall that gets whole buildings into the solar conversation, without requiring anyone to overhaul the roof, is a reasonable candidate for that.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

articles.title: Protecting Earth’s fragile biodiversity takes spotlight at Armenia talks
articles.summary: Biodiversity losses continue to upend the lives of billions of people whose future prosperity depends on countries taking urgent action to protect our planet, the top UN official leading talks at the UN Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan, said on Monday.
articles.content:
The aim of the talks in the Armenian capital is to assess progress so far and build on an agreed blueprint for biodiversity protection known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted four years ago.

Tweet URL

“In 2022, 196 countries made commitments. But we are all accountable to each other and to future generations. What happens here in Yerevan matters. Billions of people whose lives are being upended by the impacts of biodiversity loss depend on progress being made here in the next two weeks,” said Executive Secretary of the UN Convention on Biodiversity, Astrid Schomaker.

Tapping into indigenous ideas

Insisting that “taking action for nature does work”, Ms. Schomaker called for the “untapped energy and ideas” of Indigenous Peoples and local communities, women and youth to contribute to the decisions made at the talks. “We need even greater engagement from cities, businesses and financial institutions…the science is clear. No nation, no economy, no society is immune from the impacts of biodiversity loss,” she said.

The goals of the Convention include tackling the main drivers of biodiversity loss, including changes in how land and seas are used, the unsustainable exploitation of species, climate change, pollution and invasive species.

Perhaps the Kunming-Montreal framework’s best-known ambition is “30 by 30”: conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030, the deadline for achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

To do this, national action plans must align with international goals, finance must match current needs and consumption and production should be in accord with “the finite resources of our planet”, Ms. Schomaker maintained.

Why do these talks matter?

A core aim of the Yerevan talks – also known as COP17, or the 17th Conference Of Parties – is “to turn commitments into measurable progress on the ground”, insisted Armenia’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Paruyr Hovhannisyan.

“We want COP17 to send a clear political signal that addressing biodiversity loss requires coordinated action by governments, international organizations, the private sector and civil society,” he told UN News. “This means strengthening implementation, mobilizing adequate resources, and improving monitoring and accountability.”

Among the big issues governments will grapple with in Yerevan:

Taking stock: Countries will conduct the very first global review of collective progress under the framework by presenting their national reports and updated national biodiversity strategies and action plans. This will show what has been achieved since 2022 and where faster action is needed.

This will show what has been achieved since 2022 and where faster action is needed. Closing the implementation gap: The question is how to translate national targets and plans into measurable results on the ground.

The question is how to translate national targets and plans into measurable results on the ground. Finding the money: The framework calls for at least $200 billion annually from all sources by 2030 , including at least $30 billion in international biodiversity finance, according to Armenia’s UN Ambassador Mr. Hovhannisyan.

Making the Cali Fund work: This global financial mechanism established under the UN Convention on Biodiversity was agreed at COP16 in Cali, Colombia. Talks at Yerevan aim to advance practical arrangements for the fund, which was designed to collect funds from companies that use digital genetic data and redistribute these monies to protect biodiversity and Indigenous Peoples.

Tracking progress: Better monitoring, data, capacity and cooperation are needed so countries can measure whether commitments are actually delivering results.

Changing the economics: Some of the areas furthest behind require action outside environment ministries, including on finance, business, sustainable consumption and harmful incentives.

The meeting follows warnings from UN chief António Guterres in Yerevan on Friday that more than one million species face extinction.

War on nature

In his call for an end to the “war on nature”, the UN Secretary-General appealed to governments, business and communities to accelerate efforts to protect biodiversity for future generations.

“Every day, humankind saws another branch through the tree of life. Climate chaos, invasive species, overgrazing and overfishing, excessive fertilizers, pesticides, plastics and heavy metals, all these and more are driving the triple planetary crisis of pollution, biodiversity loss and climate chaos,” he said.

The UN chief warned that the world is edging ever closer towards becoming uninhabitable. But he also pointed to international biodiversity action agreed under the Kunming-Montreal Framework .

It had inspired action worldwide, Mr. Guterres insisted, noting that since 2022, an additional 1.3 million square kilometres of land and six million square kilometres of ocean have received formal protection.

But “progress is uneven and far too slow” and countries risk falling “well short” of the goal of conserving 30 per cent of the world’s land and sea by 2030, the UN chief said.

articles.personality_title: UN talks in Armenia push to protect 30% of Earth’s land and sea by 2030
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The world is losing many plants, animals, and natural places, which affects billions of people. To stop this, countries agreed on a plan called the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework four years ago. Now, they are meeting in Yerevan, Armenia, to check progress and make stronger plans.

**What happened** – From June 2024, leaders and experts from nearly 200 countries gathered at the 17th Conference of Parties (COP17) to discuss how well they are protecting nature. They reviewed reports on what has been done since 2022 and talked about how to turn promises into real actions. They also discussed ways to raise money, including a special fund to help protect biodiversity and support Indigenous Peoples.

**Impact** – This meeting is important because it focuses on saving 30% of the Earth’s land and oceans by 2030. This goal helps protect homes for many species and supports people who depend on nature. The talks also bring in ideas from Indigenous Peoples, women, and young people, showing that everyone’s voice matters. Countries agreed that protecting nature is connected to fighting climate change and pollution.

**What's next step** – After this meeting, countries will need to improve their plans, share better information, and find enough money to meet their goals. They will also work on making sure businesses and governments follow through. The success of these talks will be measured by how much land and sea get protected and how well the plans are carried out.

**One-sentence takeaway** – At the UN conference in Armenia, nearly 200 countries are working together to protect 30% of Earth’s land and oceans by 2030 through stronger actions, funding, and cooperation.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les négociations de l’ONU en Arménie visent à protéger 30 % des terres et océans d’ici 2030
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le monde perd de nombreuses plantes, animaux et espaces naturels, ce qui affecte des milliards de personnes. Pour arrêter cela, les pays ont adopté un plan appelé le Cadre mondial pour la biodiversité de Kunming-Montréal il y a quatre ans. Maintenant, ils se réunissent à Erevan, en Arménie, pour faire le point et renforcer leurs plans.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Depuis juin 2024, des dirigeants et experts de près de 200 pays se sont réunis à la 17e Conférence des Parties (COP17) pour discuter de la protection de la nature. Ils ont examiné les rapports sur les actions menées depuis 2022 et ont parlé de la manière de transformer les promesses en actions concrètes. Ils ont aussi discuté des moyens de lever des fonds, y compris un fonds spécial pour protéger la biodiversité et soutenir les peuples autochtones.

**Impact** – Cette réunion est importante car elle vise à sauver 30 % des terres et océans d’ici 2030. Cet objectif aide à protéger les habitats de nombreuses espèces et soutient les personnes qui dépendent de la nature. Les discussions intègrent aussi les idées des peuples autochtones, des femmes et des jeunes, montrant que chaque voix compte. Les pays ont reconnu que protéger la nature est lié à la lutte contre le changement climatique et la pollution.

**Prochaine étape** – Après cette réunion, les pays devront améliorer leurs plans, partager de meilleures informations et trouver suffisamment d’argent pour atteindre leurs objectifs. Ils travailleront aussi à faire respecter les engagements par les entreprises et les gouvernements. Le succès sera mesuré par la part des terres et océans protégés et la mise en œuvre des plans.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Lors de la conférence de l’ONU en Arménie, près de 200 pays collaborent pour protéger 30 % des terres et océans d’ici 2030 grâce à des actions renforcées, un financement accru et une meilleure coopération.
articles.personality_title_es: Las negociaciones de la ONU en Armenia buscan proteger el 30 % de tierras y mares para 2030
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El mundo está perdiendo muchas plantas, animales y lugares naturales, lo que afecta a miles de millones de personas. Para detener esto, los países acordaron un plan llamado Marco Mundial de Biodiversidad de Kunming-Montreal hace cuatro años. Ahora se reúnen en Ereván, Armenia, para revisar los avances y fortalecer sus planes.

**Qué pasó** – Desde junio de 2024, líderes y expertos de casi 200 países se reunieron en la 17ª Conferencia de las Partes (COP17) para hablar sobre cómo proteger la naturaleza. Revisaron informes sobre lo logrado desde 2022 y discutieron cómo convertir promesas en acciones reales. También hablaron sobre cómo conseguir fondos, incluyendo un fondo especial para proteger la biodiversidad y apoyar a los pueblos indígenas.

**Impacto** – Esta reunión es importante porque busca salvar el 30 % de las tierras y océanos para 2030. Esta meta ayuda a proteger el hogar de muchas especies y apoya a las personas que dependen de la naturaleza. Las conversaciones también incluyen ideas de pueblos indígenas, mujeres y jóvenes, mostrando que todas las voces cuentan. Los países reconocieron que proteger la naturaleza está conectado con luchar contra el cambio climático y la contaminación.

**Próximo paso** – Después de esta reunión, los países deberán mejorar sus planes, compartir mejor información y encontrar suficiente dinero para lograr sus objetivos. También trabajarán para asegurar que empresas y gobiernos cumplan. El éxito se medirá por cuánto territorio se protege y cómo se implementan los planes.

**Frase clave** – En la conferencia de la ONU en Armenia, casi 200 países trabajan juntos para proteger el 30 % de las tierras y océanos para 2030 mediante acciones más fuertes, financiamiento y cooperación.
